name: Barium Yellow
lede: Barium yellow is the old pigment name for barium chromate, a light, greenish yellow that went by half a dozen trade names.

sections.title: The pigment
sections.body:
Barium yellow is barium chromate, a light yellow pigment [1][2]. The Pigment Compendium gives its chemical formula as BaCrO4 and lists it among the barium compounds that make colors [3].

Trade catalogs sold it, pure or mixed, under a crowd of aliases, among them baryta yellow, Steinbühl yellow and the misleading "ultramarine yellow", as well as lemon yellow and permanent yellow [2][4]. The name "yellow ultramarine" is a trade label only; the compound is a chromate, not the blue mineral pigment [2][3]. The shared names matter when you read old paint catalogs: [[lemon-yellow]] on a label may mean this pigment, and "permanent yellow" was used for it too [4].

sections.title: A modern yellow
sections.body: One book on color and memory groups barium yellow with lemon yellow among the modern yellows that resist light, and dates them to the early nineteenth century [5]. That is a loose, literary source, so treat the date as approximate. A later chemical note records that a paint based on barium potassium chromate, made to resist corrosion, was developed in the 1940s [4]. An artists' reference of 1928 is cited for the shorter name "barium chrome" [4].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch comes from Ridgway's 1912 color atlas, plate XVI, and the 1955 ISCC-NBS system calls the nearest block "moderate yellow", only 2.2 units of color difference away [6]. Ridgway's plates are aged scans, so the hex is approximate [6]. This is a pale, soft yellow, much lighter and less saturated than a full [[yellow]] [6].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The ColorHub name archive files barium yellow under the yellows, with a lightness of 90 out of 100, so it sits near the top of the lightness scale among named colors [6]. Contrast against white is only 1.28 to 1, so text in this color on white is unreadable [6].

origin.first_recorded: Ridgway, 1912 (as a color name); pigment c. early 19th century, loosely dated

choices: A mix of cadmium and sulfur

questions.q: True or false: "yellow ultramarine" is a blue pigment.

openers: Barium yellow also sold as lemon yellow, permanent yellow and yellow ultramarine, all names for one chromate.

issues: Lede called it a pale, cool lemon yellow; the sources say light yellow (Colour Index: dull, greenish yellow). Reworded.
